newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka parties to work together on ending war.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka parties to work together on ending war.

text.p: Sri Lanka's ruling People's Alliance and the main opposition United National Party (UNP) have agreed to work together to try to end the long war against Tamil rebels, the government said on Thursday.

Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Lakshman Kadirgamar said in a statement on behalf of President Chandrika Kumaratunga and opposition leader Ranil Wickremesinghe that the two parties were aiming at a "common approach" to solve the crisis.

"The president and the leader of the opposition have exchanged letters about a number of arrangements which are intended to develop a common, cross-party approach -- a bipartisan approach -- towards the resolution of the ethnic conflict in our country," Kadirgamar said in his statement, which he read at a news conference.
Kadirgamar said Britain had played an important role in the settlement between the two parties.

He said he had extensive discussions with British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind and the Under-Secretary of State Liam Fox in recent months about Britain's common political approach to the problem in Northern Ireland.
"Dr Fox's advice about this experience has proved to be most useful," Kadirgamar said in his statement. He did not give further details.

The two Sri Lankan leaders, in similar letters to each other, agreed that the head of the government would seek the opinion of the opposition leader on significant developments relating to the ethnic conflict, regardless of the party in power.

They also agreed that the party in opposition would not undermine any discussions or decisions between the ruling party and any other group, including the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels, aimed at ending the ethnic conflict.
"The development of a genuinely bipartisan approach to the resolution of the ethnic conflict is vital to the achievement of a permanent solution to the conflict," the letters said.
Sri Lankan forces have fought for 13 years against the LTTE, which demands a separate homeland for minority Tamils in the island's north and east.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the conflict. The LTTE says the number is higher.

"The need to restore peace is of overwhelming importance, for progress in other areas in our country and for the prosperity of our people. It is a need that transcends party politics," Kadirgamar said.

Rifkind visited Sri Lanka last August. Fox has visited the island three times in recent months, the last time on Wednesday when he flew into Colombo for a 24-hour visit during which he met Kadirgamar and Wickremesinghe.

Political sources said Fox had asked Wickremesinghe whether he would oppose talks between the LTTE and the government and the opposition leader reportedly agreed to take steps to work with the government if talks were initiated with the rebels.
An LTTE spokesman in London was not immediately available for comment.
